title: OPTIMJACK web supply-chain attack hit nearly 180 websites with crypto-wallet swapping and card skimming
description:
Unit 42 says the OPTIMJACK attack reached nearly 180 websites with scripts for crypto-wallet address swapping, card skimming and exploit kits, and Mandiant says malicious loaders served from trusted CDNs from Nov 13 to 16 stole cards, cookies and crypto. title: Update: Jensen Huang says he would return as Nvidia CEO if the board asks, but the board reportedly is not looking to reinstate him

Why it matters: Nvidia's leadership is now an open question hours before an earnings call that will be read as a test of the AI buildout.

In an unusual joint statement, Commerce and the Justice Department said Commerce began investigating Megaspeed in 2024 and requested Nvidia's sales records in May 2025, Nvidia put Megaspeed on its "no sell" list in June 2025, and DOJ then took over a criminal investigation. As summarized on the list, the statement does not accuse Huang or Nvidia of wrongdoing.

Why it matters: The case ties Huang's exit to US efforts to stop advanced chips from reaching Chinese state-backed AI projects.

Artificial Analysis says the top score on its Progress Index has more than doubled since the first GTA VI trailer in December 2023, from 160 to 358, with the top score beaten 23 times (about 324 likes, 19,000 views). A new top score arrived every 92 days on average in 2024, every 41 days in 2025 and every 32 days so far in 2026. Ethan Mollick adds that, contrary to many expectations, no Fable-class open model has appeared more than eight months after Fable/Mythos was first made public (about 309 likes).

Why it matters: Faster record-setting shortens every model's time at the top, and the open-closed gap decides who can build at the frontier.

title: High-Speed Insect Brain Provides Evidence of Engineering Design
description:
Two recently published studies of fly behavior provide evidence for sophisticated sensory information processing in insect brains. A study of fruit flies (Drosophila) led by scientists from the University of Sheffield examined the processing of visual information in the brain.1 When attempting to understand information processing in brains, the paradigm has been that scientists, “Often rely on stationarity assumptions and reductionist behaviour or reductionist brain activity analyses.” However, this new research shows that these assumptions are too simplified, and that the processing is much more complex. Tristan Harris worked at Google before devoting his life to saving humanity from AI. If half of what he says is true, we need to drop everything and fix this.



(00:00) Is AI Doomerism a Psyop?

Tristan is Co-Founder of the Center for Humane Technology (CHT), a nonprofit organization whose mission is to align technology with humanity’s best interests. He regularly briefs heads of state, technology CEOs, and US Congress members, in addition to mobilizing millions of people around the world through mainstream media. Tristan has explored the influences that hijack human attitudes, behaviors, and beliefs, from his childhood as a magician to his coursework in Stanford’s Persuasive Technology Lab to his leadership as a Design Ethicist at Google. Today, he studies how major technology platforms wield dangerous power over our ability to make sense of the world and leads the call for systemic change. title: Sean Stone’s 10 Things to Learn: Ancient Wisdom for the Modern Soul
description:
10 Things to Learn: Ancient Wisdom for the Modern Soul explores what it means to remain fully human in an age increasingly defined by technology, optimization, and artificial intelligence. While modern civilization has expanded humanity’s power and capability, it has done little to eliminate suffering, grief, fear, or the search for meaning. This book argues that life’s deepest questions cannot be answered through efficiency or control. Instead, genuine growth emerges through a series of essential initiations—moments of collapse, surrender, loss, rest, and devotion that shape the soul. Blending mythology, philosophy, memoir, and poetic reflection, it offers a timeless framework for navigating the emotional and spiritual disorientation of modern life.

Structured around ten symbolic “gates,” the book reframes life as a cyclical journey of awakening rather than a linear pursuit of success. These gates—Falling, Surrendering, Crying, Caring, Hating, Creating, Sharing, Loving, Breathing, and Laughing—each represent a threshold of psychological and spiritual transformation. Drawing from Greek mythology, Biblical narratives, Eastern philosophy, and archetypal storytelling, the book presents a unified map of human development. Its voice combines lyrical prose with intellectual rigor, placing it at the intersection of Joseph Campbell’s mythological insight, Alan Watts’s spiritual inquiry, and the literary introspection of Hermann Hesse.

At a time of accelerating technological change, rising anxiety, and the erosion of traditional sources of meaning, 10 Things to Learn offers something increasingly rare: not just insight, but initiation. It speaks to readers seeking coherence in a fragmented world and restores a sense of purpose through the defining ordeals of the human experience.

Nate Soares is President of the Machine Intelligence Research Institute (MIRI), where he has led AI safety research for more than a decade following engineering roles at Google and Microsoft. He is the co-author, alongside Eliezer Yudkowsky, of the New York Times bestselling book If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies: Why Superhuman AI Would Kill Us All (2025), which argues that the current race to develop super intelligent AI will end catastrophically unless humanity globally coordinates to stop it.

Nate has published extensively on AI alignment, including foundational work on decision theory, goal specification, and the incentives that drive advanced AI systems to seek power in ways their creators neither anticipate nor intend.
